name: Sultanate of Sulu
summary: A Muslim Tausug sultanate in the Sulu Archipelago, with power reaching Palawan and north-eastern Borneo. It thrived on sea trade and resisted Spain for centuries.

location.value: The Sulu Archipelago, parts of Zamboanga and Palawan, and north-eastern Borneo (Sabah).

terrain.value: The Sulu Archipelago of volcanic and coral islands between Mindanao and Borneo, surrounded by shallow seas and reefs.

climate.value: Equatorial: hot and wet all year, mostly south of the main typhoon belt.

disasters.value: Typhoons are rare this far south; earthquakes and tsunamis (such as the 1897 Mindanao earthquake) occurred.

population.value: No reliable estimate; perhaps around 100,000 or more in the 18th–19th centuries.

urbanisation.value: Jolo was the capital and a busy port with a market for traders from many countries.

disease.value: Unknown in detail; smallpox and cholera spread through trading ports.

migration.value: Captives from raids were brought to Sulu.

economicBase.value: Sea trade and collection of marine products for China.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with China, Borneo and the British.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Trade in pearls, sea cucumbers and slaves; Spanish silver dollars and Chinese goods were used in exchange.

governmentType.value: A sultanate in which the sultan shared power with powerful local chiefs (datus).

keyRulers.value: Sharif ul-Hashim (founder, 1405 or 1457), Jamalul Kiram II (last ruling sultan).

succession.value: Sultans were chosen from the royal family by a council of datus, which often led to disputes.

institutions.value: Islamic law (with local custom), a council of datus, and religious officials.

stability.value: Lasted about five centuries despite three centuries of wars with Spain.

eliteConflict.value: Rival datus and claimants to the throne competed for power and trade.

armyAndTech.value: Fast outrigger warships (lanong) and swords such as the kris and barong; cannons from traders.

majorWars.value: The long Moro Wars with Spain (16th–19th centuries); the Moro Rebellion against the US (1899–1913).

territoryChange.value: Gained north-east Borneo from Brunei in the 17th century.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival of Spain; dealt with Britain, which leased North Borneo from Sulu in 1878.

inventions.value: Little is known; skilled boat-building and pearl diving.

scienceEducation.value: Islamic learning in mosques and Qur’an schools.

openness.value: Traded widely with Chinese, British and other merchants, especially in the 18th century.

communicationTransport.value: Outrigger boats and fast warships connected the islands.

religion.value: Sunni Islam, brought by traders and missionaries from the late 14th century.

languageWriting.value: Tausug, written in the Arabic-based Jawi script; Malay was used in diplomacy.

artsArchitecture.value: Okir carving with flowing plant designs; decorated boats and weapons.

socialStructure.value: Sultan, datus, commoners and slaves (often captured in raids).

sharedIdentity.value: A Tausug Muslim identity, distinct from the Christian north of the Philippines.

dailyLife.value: Houses on stilts over water; fish, cassava and rice.

neighbours.value: The Sultanate of Brunei, the Sultanate of Maguindanao, Spanish Philippines and British Borneo.

ideasReligions.value: Helped spread Islam in the southern Philippines and northern Borneo.

colonisation.value: The sultan gave up political power to the US in 1915.

peakPeriod.value: The late 18th century, when trade with China and British merchants boomed.

declineSignals.value: Spanish attacks (Jolo was taken in 1876) and then US rule weakened the sultan.

outcome.value: The sultan gave up political power to the US in 1915; the royal title continues today.

sources.value: Tarsila genealogies. Checked against Wikipedia (“Sultanate of Sulu”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium; the founding date is 1405 or 1457.
